questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with 4 weeks of fevers, weight loss, and chronic diarrhea. The patient reported intermittent diffuse abdominal pain, 5 to 6 watery, nonbloody bowel movements/day. She endorsed a 20 lb weight loss over this same duration. She was known to have HIV but was not taking HIV medications or antibiotic prophylaxis. On examination there was diffuse abdominal tenderness but no peritoneal signs. Shotty axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy was palpable. Investigations: CD4 count 30 cells/μL HIV viral load 110,350 copies/mL Mycobacterial blood cultures: positive with AFBs at 7 days; DNA probe negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Clarithromycin, ethambutol, and rifabutin The most likely infection to cause this clinical presentation of fevers, diarrhea, and wasting in an advanced AIDS patient with positive AFB blood cultures is disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease. The recommended treatment is a macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin), ethambutol, plus an optional third agent in severe cases or patients failing ART (typically rifabutin).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q39

questions.stem: An outbreak of diarrhea was linked to a local water park. Before the cases were linked to a common source, patients were seen by a variety of providers, and a number of investigations performed. Investigations: Stool microscopy: small, round cysts seen on acid-fast stain Colon biopsy: small cysts are seen that appear to be sitting on the surface of the colonic epithelium
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium sp. Cryptosporidium is the smallest of the coccidian parasites that are acid fast. While Cryptosporidium is an intracellular parasite it often appears to be sitting on the surface of the epithelium. Cyclospora is also acid fast but is twice the size of Cryptosporidium and will be in the cytoplasm of enterocytes. Cystoisospora is the largest of the coccidian parasites and will also be in the cytoplasm of enterocytes. Giardia is not acid fast and is a parasite of the small intestine where the trophozoites are attached to the mucosal surface but are not intracellular. Enterocytozoon is smaller than Cryptosporidium, is intracellular, but is not acid fast.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q20

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of diarrhea, malaise, abdominal pain, nausea, and flatulence. She was opening her bowels on average 12 times per day. There was no blood or mucus. She attended a regular swimming class with her 9-month-old daughter, and the pool had been closed one week earlier after an outbreak of diarrhea. Stool microscopy: multiple red oocysts, 4–6 μm diameter seen on modified acid-fast stain.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Nitazoxanide The pathogen here is Cryptosporidium; first-line treatment is with nitazoxanide.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q37

questions.question: Recreational water exposure.

parts.text: Give two causes of infectious dermatitis from hot tub exposure.
Give one (or two) causes of pneumonia from hot tub exposure.
What is the most common parasitic cause of widespread waterborne diarrheal illness?

parts_raw.text: 2 causes of infectious dermatitis from hot tub exposure?
1 (or 2) causes of pneumonia from hot tub exposure
Most common parasitic cause of widespread waterborne diarrheal illness?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Pseudomonas aeruginosa hot tub folliculitis (also hot hand-foot syndrome/green nail syndrome). (2) Nontuberculous mycobacteria (Mycobacterium avium complex). b) (1) Mycobacterium avium complex hypersensitivity pneumonitis ('hot tub lung'). (2) Legionella pneumophila. c) Cryptosporidium species - the most frequent pathogen implicated in recreational-water outbreaks and a leading parasitic cause of waterborne diarrhea (Giardia is the other principal cause).
questions.beyond_mandell: Hot tub lung (MAC hypersensitivity pneumonitis), Legionella, and nontuberculous mycobacterial dermatitis are not in this Pseudomonas chapter; that content rests on general/PHAC-CDC waterborne-disease knowledge.
questions.cohort_conflict: The chapter identifies Cryptosporidium as the most frequent recreational-water pathogen, so for waterborne illness Cryptosporidium is favored over the cohort's Giardia.

cohort_answer.text: Dermatitis: Hot tub folliculitis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) - painful pruritic pustules within 24-48h, self-resolves 7-14d; Hot foot syndrome (Pseudomonas) - painful red nodular lesions on soles, self-limiting 7-10d; Green nail syndrome (pseudomonas) with onychomycosis; Mycobacterium species. Pneumonia: MAC hypersensitivity pneumonitis ('hot tub lung'), usually self-limiting, may need prednisone +/- antimycobacterial; Legionellosis (usually L. pneumophila). Parasite: Giardia lamblia (most common cause of parasitic diarrhea worldwide; cryptosporidium also very high incidence); tx metronidazole/tinidazole/nitazoxanide, paromomycin if pregnant first trimester

questions.question: The current algorithm for intestinal parasites includes direct smears plus a concentration step and then an iron-hematoxylin (permanent trichrome-type) stain.
questions.question_raw: Current algorithm for intestinal parasites includes direct smears as well as concentrate and then iron hematoxylin stain.

parts.text: Name 4 clinically significant intestinal parasites that can be missed by this algorithm and 1 stain for each that you would use to detect them.

parts_raw.text: Name 4 clinically significant intestinal parasites that can be missed by this algorithm and 1 stain for each that you would use for them.

questions.model_answer: a) The routine ova-and-parasite algorithm (direct smear + formalin-ethyl-acetate concentration + iron-hematoxylin/trichrome permanent stain) does not reliably detect the intestinal coccidia or microsporidia, because their oocysts/spores stain poorly with iodine or trichrome and resemble yeast. Four missed pathogens and a dedicated stain for each: (1) Cryptosporidium spp. - modified acid-fast stain (modified Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun; oocysts stain pink/red on a green-blue background), or auramine-rhodamine fluorescent stain / direct immunofluorescence. (2) Cyclospora cayetanensis - modified acid-fast stain (variably acid-fast; also autofluoresces under UV). (3) Cystoisospora (Isospora) belli - modified acid-fast stain. (4) Microsporidia (e.g., Enterocytozoon bieneusi, Encephalitozoon intestinalis) - modified trichrome stain (chromotrope 2R / Weber stain) or calcofluor white.
questions.beyond_mandell: Cyclospora, Cystoisospora and the microsporidian-specific stains (chromotrope 2R / calcofluor white) are established diagnostic practice (CDC DPDx; Mandell parasite-diagnosis chapters) rather than detailed in this Cryptosporidium chapter, which names acid-fast staining for Cryptosporidium and notes acid-fast stains also detect Cystoisospora and Cyclospora.
